title: Spare tempi
summary: Pawn endings: whoever has a pawn move to spare wins the zugzwang fight.
part.pass.title: One move to spare
part.pass.summary: When the side to move loses, a pawn move hands the move to the other side.
part.count.title: Counting tempi
part.count.summary: Both sides have pawn moves: whoever has more wins.
part.double.title: One step or two
part.double.summary: A pawn on its starting square can give two tempi, if it moves one square at a time.
part.timing.title: At the right moment
part.timing.summary: First the king takes its post; the spare tempo is kept for the end.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: Two rules, the defence, and an ending to play.
step.t_pass: White to move. Each king attacks the other pawn and defends its own. Whoever steps away gives up his pawn. What does White do here?
step.t_pass.hint1: Picture the position without the a2-pawn. Whoever had the move would be lost. So you want Black to be the one moving.
step.t_pass.hint2: There is a white piece that can move without spoiling anything on the kingside.
step.treb: A reminder from the mined-squares lesson: without the a2-pawn, this position is the trébuchet. Each king attacks the other pawn, and whoever has the move loses.
step.spare: Now put the a2-pawn back. It attacks nothing, defends nothing and is far from everything. Still, it decides the game: 1.a3 or 1.a4 changes nothing near the kings and hands the move to Black. A move like that is called a spare tempo. In a pawn ending it can be worth as much as an extra pawn.
step.d_pass: Watch what happens when Black gets the move.
step.d_pass.m1: 1.a3. The waiting move. The kingside stays the same, but now Black has to move.
step.d_pass.m2: 1...Kd3. The black king has no good square: every move drops the f5-pawn or stops attacking f4.
step.d_pass.m3: 2.Kxf5. The pawn falls, and my king still guards the f4-pawn.
step.d_pass.m4: 2...Ke3. The black king attacks f4, but the pawn is protected.
step.d_pass.m5: 3.a4. Now there are two passed pawns, one on the f-file and one on the a-file, far apart. The black king cannot hold both.
step.passMove: White to move and win. Pass the move.
step.passMove.hint: Leave the king alone: it is on its best square. Use the piece that can move without changing anything on the kingside.
step.passMove.done: That's it. The pawn moved, and now the black king has to drop the f5-pawn or stop attacking f4. 1.a3 worked too. King moves only drew: here the pawn is what passes the move.
step.t_count: White to move. The same trébuchet, but now Black also has an a-pawn. Who wins here?
step.t_count.hint1: Count the pawn moves each side can still make before the a-pawns lock.
step.t_count.hint2: If each side answers the other's pawn move with a pawn move, who runs out first?
step.equal: Here the count is even: the a2-pawn and the a7-pawn share the same squares, a3, a4, a5 and a6. For each pawn move of mine, Black has an answer, and whoever moves first runs out first. With White to move, White loses. If the number of empty squares is odd, the count turns in favour of the side to move: with the black pawn on a6 and White to move, for example, White moves one square only, 1.a3!, and then answers each move of the black pawn. Spare tempi only count when one side has more than the other.
step.d_equal: Now with Black to move. The same count, but this time Black runs out.
step.d_equal.m1: 1...a6. Black spends a tempo. If Black played 1...a5 at once, I would answer 2.a4 and the pawns would lock with Black to move.
step.d_equal.m2: 2.a3. I answer with one square. 2.a4 here would be a mistake: Black would play 2...a5 and make the last move.
step.d_equal.m4: 3.a4. The pawns are locked, and the last pawn move was mine.
step.d_equal.m5: 3...Kd4. With no pawn moves left, the black king must step away.
step.d_equal.m6: 4.Kxf5. The pawn falls and the game is won.
step.extra: Now White has two queenside pawns, a2 and b2, against one, a7. Both sides have tempi, but one has more. The side with more waiting pawn moves wins the fight. Just don't spend the wrong one: a pawn that can be captured doesn't pass the move.
step.extraMove: White to move and win. Spend the tempi one at a time, without leaving Black with the last one.
step.extraMove.hint: Answer each black pawn move with a pawn move of your own. Watch out for a pawn that steps onto a square where it can be taken.
step.extraMove.done: Well done. Black ran out of pawn moves first, and the black king has to drop the f5-pawn. After 1.b3 a5, 2.b4? lost: 2...axb4 and the tempo is gone.
step.t_double: White to move. Until now the spare pawn moved once. This position, from a study by DrMkcTheHandsome, needs two waiting moves. The kings face each other with one square between them, and whoever has the move must give way. White has a pawn on c2, still on its starting square. How does White use that pawn?
step.t_double.hint1: How many times will White need to pass the move before the end?
step.t_double.hint2: A pawn on its starting square can move one square or two. How many waiting moves does it give in each case?
step.t_double.hint3: You will need to pass the move now, and again when the king reaches e5.
step.noReserve: First, the position without the c2-pawn. The kings are on e4 and e6, face to face, and White is to move: White has to retreat or step aside, and the black king advances. With no reserve, this position is lost for White. The c2-pawn is there to change that.
step.d_double: The right way, one square at a time.
step.d_double.m1: 1.c3! Just one square. The pawn passes the move and still keeps one move for later.
step.d_double.m2: 1...Kf7. The black king retreats. It has no better square.
step.d_double.m3: 2.Ke5. My king advances to e5. The black king will answer by stepping in front of it, and then the move is mine again.
step.d_double.m4: 2...Ke7. Now the kings face each other, and it is my move. Without the second tempo, it would be a draw.
step.d_double.m5: 3.c4! The pawn's second tempo. Now Black has to move.
step.d_double.m6: 3...Kd7. The black king steps aside and gives up the f6-square.
step.d_double.m7: 4.Kf6. The king gets in and attacks the g6-pawn.
step.d_double.m8: 4...Kc7. The black king heads the other way. The g6-pawn has no defence left.
step.d_double.m9: 5.Kxg6. The pawn falls, and my g5-pawn has a clear road.
step.doubleMove: White to move and win. Use the c2-pawn twice.
step.doubleMove.hint: Move the pawn just one square now, take the king to e5, and keep the other pawn move for when the kings face each other again.
step.doubleMove.done: Perfect: 1.c3, the king to e5, and 3.c4 at the moment it was needed. On the first move, 1.Kf4 also won; 1.c4? drew.
step.t_timing: White to move. Until now the king was already in place. Now it still has to reach e5. The h2-pawn is your reserve, and Black also has an h-pawn. What comes first: the king or the pawn?
step.t_timing.hint1: The h2-pawn can answer any move of the black pawn. Whoever spends first loses that edge.
step.t_timing.hint2: The pawn waits. Which white piece is not in place yet?
step.d_timing.m1: 1.Kf4! Only the king moves. The h2-pawn stays home, with both options.
step.d_timing.m2: 1...Kc4. The black king attacks d4 and defends d5.
step.d_timing.m3: 2.Ke5. The trébuchet, with Black to move.
step.d_timing.m4: 2...h5. Black spends his tempo and hands me the move. Two empty squares are left between the pawns, h3 and h4, and the double step closes both at once.
step.d_timing.m5: 3.h4! Here the double step is right: the pawns lock with my move, and Black has none left.
step.d_timing.m6: 3...Kc3. The black king lets go of the d5-pawn.
step.d_timing.m7: 4.Kxd5, the only winning move here. The pawn falls, and White has two pawns against one.
step.timingMove: White to move and win. The king first, the pawn at the end.
step.timingMove.hint: Don't touch the h2-pawn until the king reaches e5. It is your answer to the black pawn.
step.timingMove.done: That's it. The king reached e5 with the pawn still in reserve, and Black had to drop the d5-pawn. On the last move, 3.h4 also won.
step.rules: Two rules. First: in a locked pawn ending, look for the zugzwang and count the pawn moves on both sides; whoever makes the last one passes the move and wins. Second: the king takes its post first, and the pawn on its starting square is kept for the end, because it can choose between one square and two.
step.finish: Now play it to the end. Black defends as well as possible. Keep the h2-pawn for the right moment.
ex.e02: White to move and win. There is only one square between the h-pawns.
ex.e02.hint: Whoever takes the empty square between the pawns makes the last pawn move.
ex.e02.solution: 1.h3! The pawns lock with your move, and Black, with no pawn move, must move the king. Every white king move loses.
ex.e08: White to move and win. Two pawns against one, with the black king stuck in the corner.
ex.e08.hint: The h2-pawn is your reserve. Keep its options open.
ex.e08.solution: 1.g5 (1.h3 and 1.Kh5 also win) and, after 1...Kg8, 2.h3! The h-pawn moves one square at a time and keeps its tempi for the end. 1.h4? at once draws, and on the second move only 2.h3 wins.
ex.e10: White to move and win. A real, long ending: the first move decides.
ex.e10.hint: The b2-pawn has two tempi. You will need both later.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Ke2! and 2.Kd3! The king advances and the b2-pawn stays home. 1.b3? or 1.b4? now draw; later, when the white king is close to the black one, the two tempi of the b-pawn decide.
ex.e11: White to move and win. Another zugzwang, this time on the queenside: the kings attack the b-pawns, and Black also has an h-pawn.
ex.e11.hint: The heart of the fight doesn't change: with the kings like this, whoever has the move loses. Count the empty squares between the h-pawns.
ex.e11.solution: 1.h3! and, after 1...h5, 2.h4! White makes the last pawn move, and the black king has to let go of the b5-pawn. 1.h4? at once lost: Black answers 1...h5 and keeps the last one. It is the same count as in the lesson, in a different structure.
ex.e12: White to move and draw. Now White is the one defending, with one pawn against two.
ex.e12.hint: The h2-pawn is not for spending. Here the king does the waiting.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Ke2! and, after 1...h4, 2.Kf2! Both are the only moves that hold. The king shuttles between e2 and f2 and the h2-pawn stays home: 1.h3? or 1.h4? lose at once. In defence the spare tempo counts too: spending it early hands the opponent the zugzwang he is looking for.
key.pass: The same trébuchet, but White has a spare pawn on the other side. One move with it passes the turn, and it is the black king that ends up in zugzwang.
key.drmkc: A reserve tempo at the right time: the rear pawn moves one square now and saves its second step for when the white king has moved up. Spending that tempo too early throws the win away.
history: In pawn endings, sometimes the best move would be to do nothing at all. Since you cannot pass in chess, the side with a pawn move to spare, a reserve tempo, can hand the obligation to move back to the opponent. Counting these moves is one of the most important calculations in the ending, and a pawn that can advance one square or two is worth its weight in gold, because it chooses the right moment. The German word zugzwang, the compulsion to move, already appeared in a chess magazine in 1858. In 1986 John Nunn beat Klaus Bischoff thanks to an edge pawn that had not even left its starting square: moving one square or two as needed, it left Black with no good moves.
practice: Now the two-tempo ending for real, in the practical challenge. 1.c3 first, the king forward, and 3.c4 at the right moment. Pick the time control and go.
part.nunn.title: Nunn's choice
part.nunn.summary: A pawn on its starting square chooses how far to move according to the opponent's pawn.
part.defense.title: On defence
part.defense.summary: The defender keeps tempi too: the king waits, and the pawn moves only when the count calls for it.
step.d_c4: The tempting mistake is 1.c4? It passes the move once, but the pawn jumped two squares and has no move left. Watch.
step.d_c4.m1: 1...Kf7. The black king retreats and waits.
step.d_c4.m2: 2.Ke5. My king advances. Now Black can step in front of it.
step.d_c4.m3: 2...Ke7. Black takes the opposition. Now I would need a waiting move, and the c4-pawn cannot move any more.
step.d_c4.m4: 3.Kf4. With no spare tempo, the king has to retreat.
step.d_c4.m5: 3...Ke6. The black king returns to e6.
step.d_c4.m6: 4.Ke4. Back to the start, without the spare pawn: it is a draw. The c2-pawn had two tempi, and 1.c4? spent both at once.
step.t_nunn: White to move. Until now the pawn on its starting square moved one square at a time; now the choice depends on the other side's pawn. This position comes from the analysis of a game between John Nunn and Klaus Bischoff, from 1986. The white king attacks d5; the black king defends d5 and attacks c5. Both sides have an a-pawn. What does White do?
step.t_nunn.hint1: If Black had to move now, what would Black lose?
step.t_nunn.hint2: Count the empty squares between the a-pawns.
step.t_nunn.hint3: The a2-pawn is still on its starting square: it can choose to move one square or two.
step.nb_game: This is the ending of John Nunn against Klaus Bischoff, at the Lugano Open of 1986. After a series of exchanges, this pawn ending was left. Nunn played 39.Kc3, and Bischoff resigned. The white king goes to d4, and the a2-pawn, which never left home, decides: against 39...Kc6 40.Kd4 a5, 41.a4! closes both squares at once and leaves Black without a useful pawn move. That was the position you just studied.
step.nb_other: If Black leaves the pawn on a6, with 39...Kc7 40.Kd4 Kc6, the choice changes: 41.a3!, and after 41...a5, 42.a4. On the other hand, 41.a4? would allow 41...a5 with the last move for Black. The same pawn serves both counts because it is still at home.
step.d_nunn: Without the f- and g-pawns, the count is the same. Watch the technique.
step.d_nunn.m1: 1.a4! Both empty squares vanish at once; the last pawn move is mine.
step.d_nunn.m2: 1...Kd7. With no pawn move, the black king has to let go of d5.
step.d_nunn.m3: 2.Kxd5. The pawn falls, and my king stands next to the c5-pawn.
step.d_nunn.m4: 2...Kc7. The black king blockades the c-pawn.
step.d_nunn.m5: 3.c6. The pawn advances with the king close by and pushes the black king back.
step.d_nunn.m7: 4.Kc5. My king goes after the a5-pawn, and the black king cannot let go of the c6-pawn.
step.nunnMove: White to move and win. One square or two?
step.nunnMove.hint: Count the squares between the a-pawns: you want to make the last pawn move.
step.nunnMove.done: That's it. 1.a4! closed both squares, and the black king had to let go of d5. In the analysis of Nunn's game, 41.a4! was the same move.
step.early: See what happens if White spends the pawn early, with 1.h4? Black answers 1...Kc3!, and the black king hits d4 from the other side. White has to defend the pawn with 2.Ke3, and then Black uses the tempo they kept: 2...h5!
step.early2: The pawns are locked, and White, to move, has no pawn move. The king has to leave e3 and leaves the d4-pawn undefended: the black king captures it. The spare tempo was spent too early.
step.t_def: Now White is defending, and it is White to move. The black king wants to get in on a4, b4 or c4 and win the d4-pawn. Black also has a spare tempo, the h6-pawn. How does White draw: king or pawn?
step.t_def.hint1: What is the black king threatening to do next move?
step.t_def.hint2: The h2-pawn is in no hurry: it moves only when the count of the h-pawns calls for it.
step.t_def.hint3: The black king gets in through a4, b4 or c4. Find the square from which your king watches all three.
step.defIdea: On defence, a spare tempo is worth just as much as in attack. If I spend the pawn now, the black king gets in through c4, and Black still keeps his tempo on h6. The king goes first; the h2-pawn waits for the black pawn to move, and only then does the count.
step.defError: First the mistake, 1.h3? A pawn move instead of a king move: the road through c4 stays open. After 1...Kc4!, the white king can no longer hold d4: 2.Kd2 Kxd4 3.Ke2 Ke4, and the black king, ahead of White's, will still go for the h3-pawn. Black wins.
step.d_def.m1: 1.Kb3! From b3 the king covers a4, b4 and c4 at once.
step.d_def.m2: 1...h5. Black spends a tempo to push me off b3.
step.d_def.m3: 2.h4! Now the count calls for the pawn: there are two empty squares between h2 and h5, and the double step closes both. After 2.h3?, Black would play 2...h4 and make the last pawn move.
step.d_def.m4: 2...Ka5. With no pawn moves left, the black king tries to get in through a4.
step.d_def.m5: 3.Ka3! The only move: my king faces the black king and covers a4 and b4.
step.d_def.m6: 3...Kb5. Any other move would lose for Black; the king goes back.
step.d_def.m7: 4.Kb3! And I go back to b3. The king does the waiting, and nobody gets in: it is a draw.
step.defMove: White to move and draw. The king first, the pawn at the right moment.
step.defMove.hint: Use the king to close the squares where the black king gets in. When the black pawn moves, count the empty squares between the h-pawns.
step.defMove.done: That's it. The king closed the way in, and 2.h4! closed both empty squares with the last pawn move. On defence, a spare tempo is also something to keep until the count calls for it.
step.t_finish: White to move. Before the last ending, make the whole plan. The white king is still on e3, and the black king comes from the other side. Where does the king go, and when and how far does the h2-pawn move?
step.t_finish.hint1: What comes first: the king or the pawn?
step.t_finish.hint2: When the black pawn moves, count the empty squares before you answer.
step.rulesDefense: And on defence the same holds: the king is the one that waits, and the spare pawn moves only when the count calls for it.
